## Contents

1. Analytical objective
2. Data and derived measures
3. Univariate discovery
4. Bivariate findings
5. Statistical validation
6. Implications and next steps

::: {.notes}
This presentation summarises the technical report. The focus is not only on dashboard-style reporting, but on using visual analytics to discover distributional patterns and potential drivers of profitability and volatility.
:::

## Analytical objective

- Explore numerical and categorical distributions.
- Investigate factors associated with profitability.
- Use visual evidence and statistical validation together.
- Treat extreme losses as part of volatility, not noise to ignore.

::: {.notes}
The assignment asks for both univariate and bivariate visual analytics. I define profitability through profit and loss ratio, and volatility through spread, claim occurrence, and extreme incurred-loss behaviour.
:::

## Data and sandbox


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|measure              |value          |
|:--------------------|:--------------|
|Records              |354140         |
|Distinct insured IDs |185678         |
|Period               |2022-2023-2024 |
|Original variables   |47             |


:::
:::


- Source: Mendeley Data motor insurance portfolio.
- Tools: `tidyverse`, `ggplot2`, `readxl`, `patchwork`.
- Derived measures: profit, loss ratio, claim flag, frequency, severity.

::: {.notes}
The dataset is large enough for both descriptive and statistical analysis. I use reproducible R code so the results can be regenerated from the raw Mendeley files.
:::

## Portfolio trend


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](TH_Ex1_slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=864}
:::
:::


::: {.notes}
Premium and incurred losses both increase from 2022 to 2024. The key question is whether premium growth is sufficient to absorb the increasing loss burden.
:::

## Loss ratio worsened in 2024


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](TH_Ex1_slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=768}
:::
:::


::: {.notes}
The 2024 loss ratio is visibly higher than 2022 and 2023. This points to declining profitability, assuming expenses are not separately modelled here.
:::

## Univariate: numerical skewness


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](TH_Ex1_slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


::: {.notes}
The most important univariate pattern is claim zero-inflation and right skewness. Many records have no incurred loss, but a small number of records have very large loss ratios.
:::

## Univariate: categorical concentration


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](TH_Ex1_slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


::: {.notes}
Policy mix and bonus-score mix are concentrated. This affects interpretation: a smaller category can have a high loss ratio, but it must be evaluated against exposure size.
:::

## Policy type and profitability


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](TH_Ex1_slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=864}
:::
:::


::: {.notes}
Comprehensive products, especially COMP_N, have the highest aggregate loss ratios. Third-party-only coverage has the lowest ratio in this comparison.
:::

## Volatility by policy type


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](TH_Ex1_slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=864}
:::
:::


::: {.notes}
The boxplot uses capped loss ratio to make the spread visible. The large right tail confirms that volatility is a material feature of this portfolio.
:::

## Other risk-related segments


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](TH_Ex1_slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


::: {.notes}
Bonus score, fuel type, and circulation area all show visible differences in aggregate loss ratio. These are useful candidates for underwriting or pricing review.
:::

## Statistical validation


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|variable         |Kruskal |Chi-square |
|:----------------|:-------|:----------|
|policy_type      |<2e-16  |<2e-16     |
|bonus_score      |<2e-16  |<2e-16     |
|driver_age_band  |<2e-16  |<2e-16     |
|vehicle_age_band |<2e-16  |<2e-16     |
|fuel_type        |<2e-16  |<2e-16     |
|circulation_area |<2e-16  |<2e-16     |
|year             |<2e-16  |<2e-16     |


:::
:::


::: {.notes}
The tests show statistically significant differences across the selected segments. Because the dataset is large, I interpret these results together with visual effect size and exposure.
:::

## Brand-level screen


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](TH_Ex1_slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=864}
:::
:::


::: {.notes}
The brand chart is exploratory. It helps identify candidates for follow-up analysis, but it should not be treated as a final causal conclusion.
:::

## Implications

- Review premium adequacy for comprehensive products.
- Investigate 2024 deterioration in loss ratio.
- Use bonus score, fuel type, and circulation area as segmentation checks.
- Examine extreme losses separately from typical-policy behaviour.
- Validate any pricing action with exposure and mix-adjusted modelling.

::: {.notes}
The visual analytics process identifies where to investigate next. It does not replace actuarial modelling, but it provides a clear evidence trail for prioritising portfolio questions.
:::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
